9. WHAT WAS DONE NEXT, AND WHAT IT FOUND
=========================================
Items 2, 3 and 5 below are now done and committed. Their results change the
picture again, so they are recorded here rather than left in the commits.

THE STATE COVERAGE ALREADY EXISTED, IN A TEST NOTHING RAN. Before writing a
phase G for combiners, alpha test and stencil, it was worth checking what was
already there: metal_copy_test compares the backend against the rasteriser with
an exact memcmp across combiners at one stage and two, alpha test, stencil with
real ops, multi-texture, DXT1, DXT3, mip selection, untextured draws and dither.
It is built on Apple and registered with nothing -- out of ctest because it
needs a GPU, and with no check script, unlike metal_batch_test. So the broadest
state coverage in the tree had never been executed, which is the same shape as
the phase-A-only problem in section 2.

Run across the three arms:

    software state    FAILS at line 49 -- the depth readback after a
                      depth-tested draw, known and tracked
    hardware state    exact match
    hardware + 565    exact match

That is the strongest result of this review. Combiners, alpha test, stencil and
multi-texture are BYTE-EXACT on the hardware path, and the software path is the
one that misses. It is also the evidence the retracted 54091 was standing in
for, and a stronger claim than that ever was, because it is exact equality
rather than a tolerance.

And it narrows the remaining space sharply. Every per-draw state translation a
mission uses is now known correct in isolation on the hardware path. The wrong
image is therefore NOT a mistranslated combiner, blend factor, stencil op or
compare function. What is left is behaviour over time or at scale: the retained
surface across frames, the clear/flip interaction, the presenter round trip --
none of which any device test reaches, because they all begin from
nv2a_metal_invalidate and run a few dozen draws.

THE SWITCH SWEEP HAD TO BE WIDER THAN THE PATTERN. RECOMP_PB_EXEC is read in
four places in three spellings; the `? 1 : 0` form the handover named finds one
of them. Ten behavioural switches now go through recomp_switch_on(), which
treats "0" and empty as off and everything else as on -- the conservative
conversion, so nothing that turns a switch on today changes. RECOMP_FAKE_PAD
stays on presence and is annotated to say why: its value is meaningful (1, <n>,
`a`, `always`) and an atoi() conversion would silently disable `=a`.

I also nearly filed a fourth instance that was not one. RECOMP_OHCI_ATTACH
looked presence-tested to the pattern match, and oracle_anchor.sh's
ORACLE_NO_OHCI_ATTACH writes RECOMP_OHCI_ATTACH=0 -- which looked like a live
broken control arm. Reading the predicate rather than the grep shows it already
excludes "0" and the empty string, and main.c's two `!getenv` sites are a
default-setter, not a gate. The rule that catches counters catches greps too.


10. THE CAUSE OF THE FLICKERING CHECKERBOARD
=============================================
FOUND, AND IT IS NOT A FRAME-BOUNDARY PROBLEM AT ALL. It is one draw, and the
gate could have caught it on day one if the fixture had set one field.

base_state() builds its state with memset(0), so s.dither was 0 in every phase
of the only test that scores an image. The one code path in this renderer that
produces a literal 4x4 lattice had never been executed. That is the THIRD
fixture field found this way, after depth_func = 4 and the zeroed clip range,
and it is the one that mattered.

Set it and the paths separate at once:

                        pixels differ   beyond one step   4x4 dither cells
    software state            0                0            0 / 0
    hardware state         8192               19           77 / 857
    hardware + 565         8402               19           93 / 878

The software path becomes EXACT -- 0 of 65536, worst error 0 steps, better than
the 1 pixel it scored with dither off. Dither is not noise; it is something the
oracle does and the gate was not asking about.

THE MECHANISM. The two fragment shaders apply the dither at different stages:

    fs      shade -> blend (in shader) -> dither -> store
    fs_hw   shade -> dither -> return  -> [blend unit] -> store

The NV2A dithers at the ROP, after blending. fs does that, and so does
nv2a_texture_copy.c at its store. fs_hw hands the biased colour to the
fixed-function blend unit instead, so the +/-0.5 LSB nudge is multiplied by the
source blend factor and mixed with a destination that already carries its own
baked-in bias, instead of being applied once at quantisation.

MEASURED, NOT INFERRED, and this is the part that makes it certain:

    dither ON, blending OFF     hardware scores 0 of 65536 -- exact
    dither ON, blending ON      hardware scores 8192

The error exists only where both are active. That is the ordering and nothing
else.

AND IT IS A PATTERN, NOT MORE NOISE. The emptiest and fullest of the sixteen
4x4 dither cells hold 77 and 857 differing pixels. Coverage disagreement -- the
kind every other phase carries -- fills all sixteen evenly. An order of
magnitude apart is the dither matrix's own shape, and the test now reports that
cell range so the distinction needs no image.

That is the flickering checkerboard: a 4x4 lattice error that compounds with
each overlapping blended layer, over backgrounds that are mostly overlapping
blended layers, changing frame to frame as the camera changes how many overlap.

FIXED, with the third pipeline. Metal has no ROP-stage dither and the blend
unit runs after the fragment shader, so a draw that needs dither after blend
has to do the blend in the shader. fs_hw_blend does that and nothing else
differently: it reads the destination, blends with the same bfactor() the
software path uses, dithers after it, and leaves depth and stencil in the real
attachments where the hardware path put them.

                        before                  after
    phase A   hardware  8192 differ, 19 over      0 differ, 0 over   worst 0
              hw + 565  8402 differ, 19 over    515 differ, 0 over   worst 1
    phase F   hardware 23003 differ, 186 over     29 differ, 29 over
              hw + 565 23601 differ, 196 over    932 differ, 29 over

The hardware path is now exactly as close to the rasteriser as the software
path, on both phases, and 565's remainder is entirely within one channel step.
The lattice spread goes from 77/857 to 0/0. metal_hw_check.sh passes again, and
passes because the defect is gone rather than because nobody asked -- the
fixture still sets dither.

Selected only where needed: hw_shader_blend() is blend && dither. Blending
alone keeps the blend unit; dithering alone is already correct in fs_hw,
because with nothing after it the bias IS the last step before quantisation. So
the raster_order_group(0) it re-introduces is paid by dithered blended draws
and nothing else.

Two things that would have been silent bugs. The selector had to go into the
pipeline CACHE KEY -- two draws with identical blend state but differing dither
need different pipelines now, and keying on blend alone would have served one
the other's pipeline. And HW_CACHE went 16 -> 32, because the key gaining a
dimension can double the set and a miss is not a small slowdown: the draw is
rejected and falls back to the CPU rasteriser.

The obvious shortcut was measured and is WORSE: skipping the shader dither when
blending scores 92 pixels beyond one step against the original 19, because the
oracle dithers and the hardware path then would not.

NOT MEASURED, and it gates defaulting anything on: the frame-time cost at a
mission. The serialisation is bounded to dithered blended draws, but what
fraction of a real frame those are is unknown, and the 9.6% the hardware path
was worth should be re-taken. Also unmeasured: the magnitude of the original
defect at scale -- this is 20 blended draws and a mission has far more overlap.


11. THE FRAME-BOUNDARY TRACE, AND WHAT IT FOUND
================================================
Done before the above, and it is how the search got narrow enough to look at a
single draw again. What survives a frame, all of it in nv2a_metal.m and all for
exactly ONE surface:

    surface, stencil_surface, hw_depth_tex, hw_stencil_tex   reallocated per swap
    surface_target / depth_target + geometry + valid/dirty
    hw_pso[16] / hw_dss[16]      keyed caches, never invalidated
    texture_cache[128]           keyed by address AND a full memcmp
    ring slabs, last_command, batch_*

Reset points: the upload block (any pointer or geometry change),
nv2a_metal_sync (readback), nv2a_metal_invalidate(target) (per surface), and
nv2a_metal_discard (which took no target at all -- fixed, see below).

CONFIRMED AND FIXED. nv2a_metal_discard dropped the retained surface without
reading it back and without being told which surface the guest was clearing.
s_gpu.color_offset moves on the register write, surface_target on the next
draw, so a clear in that window names one surface and drops another. Measured
at 24848 of 65536 pixels of finished rendering lost. Latent -- default off, and
the reproducing run reports "clear discards=0" -- so nothing recorded is
affected.

CONFIRMED, NOT FIXED. nv2a_gpu_sync_range(target, bytes) is
#define'd to nv2a_metal_sync() and discards its target. Benign while one
surface is retained; wrong the moment that changes. And hw_565_on() never
consults hw_depth_tex, so a depth-texture allocation failure would leave a
B5G6R5 attachment bound while draws fall to a pipeline built for RGBA32Float --
corruption instead of a clean fallback. Not reachable in any observed run.

UNVERIFIED. The presenter reads s_snap while snapshot_surface() writes it, and
snapshot_surface() can realloc it. dev_Present runs on the render thread; I
could not establish whether the pushbuffer executor is the same thread without
a run.

ELIMINATED WITH EVIDENCE, all of which I had first proposed as causes:
  * clip-origin mismatch -- clip is +0+0 in all 1275 reports of every archived
    mission run
  * texture cache staleness -- a hit requires a full memcmp of the contents
  * pipeline/depth-state cache overflow -- pipelines=4..5, refusals=0, cache 16
  * the batches-vs-hw-draws gap of 7381 -- empty batches returning early, and
    the same 0.6-1.1% rate in all three arms
  * an unordered tile-memory race from dropping raster_order_group(0) --
    fs_hw returns float4 and takes no destination read, so there is nothing to
    race on

ON PROCESS. Four of the six hypotheses in this section died, two of them after
I had written them up as findings rather than as guesses. Nothing false reached
a commit, because each was checked -- but in a project whose recorded failure
mode is believing a number before reading what produced it, generating the
narration ahead of the evidence is the wrong order, and I did it while
reviewing a handover about exactly that. The dither result above is what the
right order looks like: predict, measure with a control (blending off), check
the shape (the lattice), then write it down.


12. WHAT IS STILL OPEN
=======================
  1. RE-TAKE THE FRAME TIME. The dither fix re-introduces raster_order_group(0)
     for dithered blended draws, and the 9.6% and 14.5% both predate it. No
     default should move until that is measured.
  2. Whether the checkerboard fully accounts for what was seen, or only the
     grid half of it. "Solid black rectangles" and "a large black band" are not
     obviously dither, and the [FB] sampler in fbcheck-on shows frames at
     203078 of 307200 nonzero pixels where the control shows 307152. A person
     playing it with the fix in is the cheapest answer.
  3. Watch refusals= in the [METAL] report at a mission. HW_CACHE is 32 now on
     an argument, not a measurement: pipelines=4..5 was measured before the key
     gained a dimension.
  4. RECOMP_SURFACE_AUDIT is built and NOT YET RUN. It answers how often a
     clear names a surface other than the held one, which decides how bad the
     discard defect would have been.
  5. Re-run the 565 A/B on the current binary, which now names its attachment.
  6. Re-run RECOMP_VSH_REUSE properly -- the original handover's item 3.
  7. The software path's metal_copy_test line 49 depth mismatch, now the only
     arm failing an exact comparison.
  8. ab_score.py's SWITCH_TOKEN covers seven switches; RECOMP_METAL_BATCH is an
     A/B arm that is not among them.

13. THE RENDERER REVIEW, AND WHAT THE RUNS COULD NOT REACH
===========================================================
THE DITHER FIX DID NOT FIX THE PICTURE. It is a real defect and it is measured
-- 8192 of 65536 pixels on the dither lattice, software path 0, now 0 on both
-- but a person watching the game reports the artefact unchanged with it in.
Section 10 stands as a correctness fix and is retracted as an explanation.

WHAT THE ARTEFACT ACTUALLY IS, measured from dumped frames rather than from a
description: large black regions, not a 4x4 lattice. Matched capture index,
same scene, RECOMP_FB_DUMP_FLIP:

    HW=0 (default)              165 black pixels of 307200
    HW=1, 565=0              30,705
    HW=1, 565=1              22,412
    HW=1 + depth ALWAYS      50,131
    HW=1 + no stencil        32,885
    HW=1 + all blends in-shader, ordered   20,144

So it is RECOMP_METAL_HW itself, not the 565 attachment, and it is not the
depth unit, the stencil unit, the blend unit or the fragment ordering -- each
was neutered in its own run and the regions stayed. The default path renders
the same frame essentially perfectly.

I also over-read one frame: black runs in it started on a 32-pixel boundary 27%
of the time, which I called tile alignment. The other frames read 0-7%, which
is chance. It is not tile-aligned; it is large regions.

WHAT READING FOUND THAT FIVE RUNS DID NOT. Neither defect is a stage that can
be switched off, which is why the bisect could not reach them:

  * THE DEPTH/STENCIL STATE CACHE KEYED ON NINE FIELDS AND ITS DESCRIPTOR READ
    ELEVEN. stencil_zfail feeds depthFailureOperation, stencil_func_mask feeds
    readMask, and neither was in the key, so two draws differing only in one of
    those were served whichever state was built first. Hardware path only: the
    software tail takes all eleven per draw and caches nothing. Measured at
    8056 of 65536 pixels against the software path's 5. Fixed, phase I.

  * DEPTH WRITES WERE NOT GATED ON THE DEPTH TEST. depthWriteEnabled read
    depth_write alone while the fragment tail derives depth_test && depth_write
    and depth_dirty is marked on the same pair. With the test off cmp is
    already ALWAYS, so an overlay with the mask still set stamped depth over
    everything it covered here and over nothing on the other path -- and
    depth_dirty was not set, so it was never read back and the next surface
    swap re-uploaded over it from stale guest RAM. Fixed, phase H.

A THIRD, RECORDED NOT FIXED: nv2a_texture_copy_blend_factor_supported allows
eight blend factors and the software bfactor implements exactly those eight,
but nv2a_metal_blend_factor maps three more -- DST_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_DST_ALPHA
and SRC_ALPHA_SATURATED. Not reachable today, because the accept test refuses
them before the sink sees them. It is a drift hazard rather than a bug: widen
the accept test and the hardware path will blend against an alpha channel that
holds the shaded alpha, or depth immediately after an upload, or does not exist
at all under 565, while the software path's bfactor falls through to default.
nv2a_metal_state.c is deliberately standalone for upstreaming, so it should not
learn about the accept test; the two lists want a comment pointing at each
other, or one shared table.

STILL UNEXPLAINED: the black regions. All three defects above are real, all
three are fixed and pinned by a phase, and NONE of them changed the picture. A
200 s run with all three in still reports 46609 and 18613 black pixels on its
two picture frames.

THE MIXED-FRAME LEAD IS NOW DEAD TOO, and it was the best one left. The
depth-ownership comment in nv2a_metal.m describes exactly this symptom -- "every
differing pixel had software 0x000000 against hardware 0xFFFFFF" -- and the
route to it is hw_depth_upload failing, which drops hw to 0 and sends draws down
the software tail without reject() ever seeing it, so refusals= stays 0 and
proves nothing. Counted in a real run:

    MIXED draws (software tail while hw on) = 0
    depth uploads failed                    = 0
    hw draws 518122, batches 522245, refusals 0, fallbacks 0, pipelines 5

Every draw took the hardware branch and no upload ever failed. The 4123 gap
between batches and hw draws is the empty-batch early return, at the same
~0.8% seen in all three arms in section 11.

WHAT IS LEFT, with everything above eliminated. Not the depth unit, the stencil
unit, the blend unit, the fragment ordering, the attachment format, the state
caches, the mixed frame, or any per-draw state translation -- metal_copy_test
puts the hardware path byte-exact against the rasteriser across combiners,
alpha test, stencil, multi-texture, DXT and mips. Every device test agrees
exactly, and a real frame does not.

That gap is the finding. Something the hardware path does is invisible to a
test that submits a few hundred draws to one retained surface and reads it back
immediately, and shows up in a frame of ~40,000 draws across three surfaces
with ~15,000 clears. The next instrument should measure the FRAME rather than
the draw: dump the surface at intervals WITHIN one frame -- RECOMP_FB_DUMP_DRAW
already exists for that -- and find the draw index at which a region that was
correct becomes black. That localises it in the guest's own draw order, which
no synthetic phase can do.


14. WHAT THE PIXELS SAY, WHICH IS NOT WHAT I HAD ASSUMED
=========================================================
The artefact is not missing draws. It is draws that RUN AND OUTPUT BLACK.

Read out of a dumped frame at native RGB565, sky rows 40-43, across a damaged
band at x=52..70 and a clean band at x=300..322:

    clean   74D1 7CF2 74D1 7CF2 ...   sky colour, alternating by one step
    damaged 0000 0000 0800 0000 ...   zero, with 0800 at some positions

0x800 is one step of red and nothing else. Its positions have period 4 in x on
one row, period 2 on the next, and none on the rows between -- which is the 4x4
Bayer matrix. So a draw covered those columns, shaded them to approximately
zero, and the ordered dither then biased some of them up by one step. Geometry
that never rendered would carry no dither at all.

THE SHAPE IS A PICKET FENCE, and that is the "grid". Columns that are >=95%
black run x = 53,55,57...69 and 165,167...201 and 225: one pixel wide, spaced
exactly two apart, every ODD column, in bands. At a distance a one-on
one-off column pattern reads as a grid, which is what a person watching it
called it. It is not tile-aligned and it is not 32-pixel anything -- I claimed
that from one frame in section 13 and the measurement here supersedes it.

WHAT THAT RULES IN. shade() is shared between the two fragment tails, byte for
byte, and so are the Params it reads and the texture buffers it samples. So
either a DIFFERENT draw covers those columns on the hardware path -- a
visibility difference -- or shade()'s inputs differ. Every visibility stage has
been neutered in its own run and the bands survived each: depth compare,
stencil, blend unit, fragment ordering, attachment format.

WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED, and is where I would look next:

  * WHICH DRAW paints them. RECOMP_FB_DUMP_DRAW captures within a frame but
    counts batches from process start, so it cannot be aimed at a scene 170 s
    in. It needs a start offset -- a few lines -- and then consecutive captures
    either side of the damaged band name the draw in the guest's own order.
  * z_cull. fs() clamps zg into [z_clip_min, z_clip_max] when z_cull is OFF and
    fs_hw does not, so the depth those two store diverges for any draw with
    ZMIN_MAX_CONTROL set to CLAMP. JSRF is recorded as using CULL, but that is
    a whole-title statement and this is a per-draw register. Counting draws with
    z_cull == 0 is one counter and has never been done.
  * Thin geometry and sample_lod. The bands sit where the scene has thin
    vertical structures, and LOD comes from dfdx/dfdy of uv. Both tails compute
    shade() before any discard_fragment(), so the derivatives ought to match --
    but fs_hw discards where fs returns the untouched destination, and that is
    the one place the two differ in a way a quad of fragments can see.

I do not know the cause. Three defects found this session are real, fixed and
pinned, and none of them is this one.


15. THE ARTEFACT, MEASURED AT GAMEPLAY AGAINST A MATCHED CONTROL
=================================================================
TWO EARLIER MEASUREMENTS IN THIS NOTE WERE OF THE WRONG THING, and a person
watching the screen caught both. Sections 13 and 14 counted "black pixels" in
frames that were the intro and a cutscene: the black bars in the intro are
GRAPHIC ELEMENTS and the black bars in a cutscene are LETTERBOXING. The 105,000
black pixels in the 65%-non-blank frames are letterbox, entirely legitimate.
The picket-fence columns in section 14 are intro art. Neither was the bug, and
every conclusion drawn from those counts is void.

The artefact is obvious at GAMEPLAY and barely present anywhere else, which is
why 200 s runs that stop at the cutscene kept missing it. Two 280 s runs, same
pad, same capture stride, same capture indices:

    DEFAULT path   clean. A gameplay frame -- player, chain-link fence,
                   buildings, HUD, ground -- is pixel-correct.
    HARDWARE path  the ground plane is cut into rectangular blocks: some black,
                   some displaced, and the magenta-and-grey HUD meter appears
                   down in the ground.

Counting strong vertical discontinuities that land on a multiple of 64 and span
at least a third of the screen:

    hardware path, all three fixes in   66 over 11 frames   6.0 per frame
    default path                         3 over  5 frames   0.6 per frame

SO THE THREE DEFECTS FIXED IN THIS SESSION ARE NOT THIS ONE. They are real,
they are pinned by phases, and the picture is unchanged.

WHAT THE SHAPE SAYS. The blocks are axis-aligned in SCREEN space while the
ground they corrupt is perspective-projected, so the corruption is in the
surface, not in the geometry. The boundaries recur at {64, 128, 192, 256, 320,
384, 448, 512, 576} -- every multiple of 64 across a 640-wide surface, in every
frame. At RGBA32Float that is exactly 1024 bytes per band; at the guest's two
bytes it is 128. And blocks carry content from ELSEWHERE in the same frame --
the HUD meter in the ground is the clearest instance -- so this is misaddressed
copying rather than lost drawing.

WHAT IS STILL NOT KNOWN: which operation misaddresses it. The upload, the
readback and the depth paths all index with the pitch the surface was captured
with, and metal_copy_test puts every per-draw state byte-exact against the
rasteriser. The 64-pixel period is the strongest clue in this whole
investigation and it has not been explained.

WHAT I WOULD DO NEXT, in order:
  1. Score a GAMEPLAY frame, not the title screen. Every gate in this tree
     scores a synthetic surface or an intro frame, which is why all of them
     pass while the game is visibly wrong. metal_hw_check.sh cannot see this.
  2. Find the source of a displaced block: cross-correlate a corrupted 64-wide
     band against the rest of the frame and read off the offset. The offset in
     pixels, or in bytes, names the addressing error directly.
  3. Only then look for the code. Three sessions of reading have not found it
     and one measurement of the offset would.


16. FOUND: ONE RENDER PASS PER DRAW, RACING ON TILE MEMORY
============================================================
THE ARTEFACT IS A 64x64 TILE MOSAIC, and RECOMP_METAL_BATCH=1 removes it.

Measured on a real gameplay recording rather than a synthetic surface. Strong
seams found by an UNRESTRICTED search -- the earlier 64-alignment claim in
section 15 came from a search that only looked at multiples of 64 and could
only find what it was looking for, which is a methodological error and is
corrected here by counting all seams and comparing against chance:

                                frames  seams  on x%64==0  expected  enrichment
    hardware, per-draw (default)    11    248       66        3.9      17.0x
    hardware, BATCHED                7     29        0        0.5       0.0x
    software control                 5    227        3        3.5       0.8x

And in a recording the seams are on a 64 grid in BOTH axes, consistently over
three frames: vertical at game x = 0, 64, 192, 256, 320, 384, 448, 640, and
horizontal at y = 128, 256, 384. That is a tile grid, not a column artefact.

THE MECHANISM. With batching off -- the default -- every draw is its own render
pass and its own command buffer: load the whole surface into tile memory, draw
one batch, store it back. A gameplay frame issues tens of thousands of those
against the same texture, and RECOMP_METAL_CB_GPU measures 664,933 command
buffers STARTING before the previous one ended, with out-of-order = 0. Tiles
therefore resolve independently and out of step, and each 64x64 tile of the
presented frame ends up holding whichever command buffer stored it last. The
result is a mosaic of moments -- which is exactly what a person watching it
described as the background being cut and jumbled, with elements moving in the
grid.

The player is coherent because it is drawn last, into whatever the surface then
holds.

WHY IT IS HARDWARE-PATH-ONLY, and why "slow but looked ok" before. The software
path serialises overdrawn fragments with raster_order_group(0). That keeps the
GPU shallow and the producer close behind it, so the per-draw passes rarely
overlap. Removing that serialisation is where the 9.6% came from, and it is
also what let the passes race.

WHY NO DEVICE TEST COULD SEE IT. metal_batch_test submits a few hundred draws
and reads back immediately; the GPU is never behind. Its own header says the
first version of the ring phase was "toothless" for exactly this reason -- "the
GPU was never actually behind" -- and the same sentence applies to every phase
in the file.

BATCHING WAS ALREADY BUILT, default off, and had only ever been argued about on
frame time, where its A/B ranges overlapped. It is a CORRECTNESS fix, and that
changes the case for defaulting it on. metal_batch_check.sh already gates
batched output against per-draw byte for byte.

AND IT WAS UNREACHABLE UNTIL TODAY. RECOMP_METAL_HW=1 with
RECOMP_METAL_BATCH=1 segfaulted on its first draw until the stale-encoder fix
earlier in this session: batch_flush() ran after `encoder` was bound, so the
draw encoded into an ended encoder. The configuration that fixes the artefact
could not be run before that.

STILL OPEN: a finer speckle remains on textured surfaces in the batched frames,
visible in the third recording as a more granular pattern. It is a smaller and
probably separate defect, and it is not tile-aligned.

NOT YET MEASURED: what batching costs or saves in frame time on the hardware
path, which is the question that decides the default.


17. THE FIX, THE GATE THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT, AND WHAT IS LEFT
==================================================================
FIXED: RECOMP_METAL_BATCH now defaults ON. One encoder for many draws instead
of a render pass per draw, which is the correct architecture as well as the
fast one -- loading and storing a whole surface through tile memory tens of
thousands of times per frame was never going to be right. =0 restores the
per-draw path and must keep working; it is the control for the whole result.

It is a CORRECTNESS default. Batching had been argued about only on frame time,
where its A/B ranges overlapped and nobody could call it, so it sat switched
off. metal_batch_check.sh already held the invariant that decides whether
turning it on is safe -- batched output byte-for-byte against per-draw on the
device test -- and it still passes.

NEW GATE: diagnostics/jsrf_first_fault/fb_score.py, because nothing here could
score a real frame. Two metrics:

  tile     strong edges landing on a grid boundary against what chance gives,
           reported as enrichment rather than a count so it tracks the artefact
           and not the scene's own detail
  speckle  isolated pixels disagreeing with ALL their neighbours -- granular
           noise with no straight edges, which `tile` cannot see

--selftest injects a known seam and known speckle and requires detection,
because a tool that cannot fail is not a gate. Run it on two arms of the same
scene with --compare; neither metric is a pass/fail alone.

Its first use settled an open question. The granular noise a person reported is
NOT a hardware-path artefact:

    software control      15806 /Mpx
    hardware per-draw     13282
    hardware batched      11686

Highest on the known-good path, lowest on the fixed one. It is the title's own
dithering and cel-shaded detail, and the fix neither introduces nor worsens it.

ALSO FIXED, and it is the reason the A/B below can be believed: the batching
switch now names itself in the [METAL] report in BOTH states, and ab_score.py's
SWITCH_TOKEN and METAL_SWITCH_RE know about it. Batch statistics used to print
only under RECOMP_METAL_CB_STATS and only when batching was on, so the OFF arm
said nothing and any comparison fell back to "assumes the environment took" --
the same hole that ran RECOMP_APU_SELFLINK_END and RECOMP_VSH_REUSE with the
feature enabled in both arms, on the switch that turned out to decide whether
the frame is correct.

WHAT IS LEFT

  0. THE DEFAULT FLIP ITSELF IS UNVERIFIED IN A REAL RUN. Every capture that
     showed batching clean passed RECOMP_METAL_BATCH=1 explicitly, and the
     frame-time A/B sets it explicitly in both arms, so nothing has yet
     exercised the new default with the variable UNSET. That is one run and it
     is the difference between "batching fixes it" and "the fix ships".
  1. FRAME TIME. Every performance number this renderer has -- the 9.6% for the
     hardware path and the 14.5% for 565 -- predates the batching default and
     predates the dither fix's raster_order_group(0) on dithered blended draws.
     An A/B of RECOMP_METAL_BATCH on the hardware path is running; until it
     lands, treat both figures as unverified rather than wrong.
  2. Re-run the 565 A/B, whose arms were never verifiable.
  3. Re-run RECOMP_VSH_REUSE properly.
  4. metal_copy_test line 49: the software path's depth readback is now the
     only arm failing an exact comparison.
  5. RECOMP_SURFACE_AUDIT is built and still has not been run.

WHAT THIS EPISODE SHOULD CHANGE ABOUT THE GATES. The defect needed tens of
thousands of draws before the GPU fell behind the producer, and every gate in
this tree submits a few hundred to one retained surface and reads it straight
back. metal_batch_test's own header already said the first version of its ring
phase was "toothless" because "the GPU was never actually behind" -- that
sentence was true of the whole file and nobody generalised it. A gate that
cannot get the GPU behind cannot see this class of defect at all, and the
answer is fb_score.py on frames from a real run, not another synthetic phase.


18. THE RESIDUAL IS REAL, AND THE METRIC THAT SAID OTHERWISE WAS WRONG
=======================================================================
RETRACTED: "the granular noise is NOT a hardware-path artefact". It is. That
claim came from fb_score.py's speckle metric, which ranked the known-good
software path as the noisiest of three arms -- and I reported the ranking as a
result instead of reading it as the metric being broken.

SETTLED BY LOOKING, at comparable surfaces rather than comparable scenes. A
flat wall on the batched hardware path carries small sharp BLACK fragments,
two to five pixels, scattered across it. The same kind of surface on the
software control is smooth and carries none. Magnifying one crop of each
answered in a minute what four metrics could not.

WHY THE METRICS COULD NOT. Every one compared arms that never reach the same
scene, because the two paths run at different speeds and a fixed pad schedule
lands them in different places. A single-frame noise rate then measures how
much flat area a scene happens to have. `tile` escaped this only because
enrichment is a ratio taken inside one frame against that frame's own seam
count; nothing about the speckle rate is.

THE SHAPE OF WHAT IS LEFT. Black, small, on flat surfaces -- the same kind of
loss as the tile mosaic, three orders of magnitude smaller. Batching removed
the 64x64 blocks by replacing a render pass per draw with one per batch, but a
batch still ends at every flush, and the flushes have not been counted. The
`use_zeta` churn is the suspect: next_depth is NULL for any draw that neither
depth-tests nor stencil-tests, so every alternation between a depth-using draw
and a depth-less one fails the retained-surface test, and that forces a sync, a
full readback, a texture reallocation and a re-upload -- each of which ends a
batch. If a frame alternates often, batching is still committing a great many
command buffers and the same race survives at a finer grain.

NEXT, AND IT IS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN A THEORY: count surface re-uploads
and batch flushes per frame at gameplay. RECOMP_METAL_RING_AUDIT already
reports surface re-uploads and RECOMP_METAL_CB_STATS reports flushes and
draws-per-flush. If flushes per frame are in the thousands, the churn is the
mechanism and the fix is to stop tearing the surface down for a draw that
simply has no depth buffer.


19. A MAGNITUDE I GOT WRONG, AND WHAT THE COUNTERS ACTUALLY SAY
================================================================
CORRECTED: "a gameplay frame issues tens of thousands of render passes". It
does not. Measured, on the per-draw path at gameplay:

    command buffers          781,703 over 9,688 frames  =  80.7 per frame
    of those, overlapping    664,933                    =  85% of them
    draws                    315,448 over the run       =  about 40 per frame
    surface re-uploads       13,543                     =  about 1.7 per frame
    ring                     267,621 reservations, 11,509 wraps,
                             0 waits, 0 fallbacks

About eighty command buffers a frame, not tens of thousands. The figure appears
in section 16, in the batch_on() comment and in two commit messages, and it is
wrong by roughly five hundred times.

THE MECHANISM IS UNAFFECTED. Eighty render passes a frame, each loading and
storing a whole surface through tile memory, with 85% of them starting before
the previous one ended, is ample to produce the tile races -- and the fix
measured 17.0x enrichment down to 0.0x. What was wrong was the scale of the
number, not the argument it supported. The two counters are also a consistency
check on each other: 781,703 command buffers at 80.7 per frame is 9,688 frames,
and 664,933 of them overlapping is the 85% above.

AND IT WEAKENS MY OWN NEXT HYPOTHESIS. Section 18 nominated the use_zeta churn
as the reason the residual specks survive batching, on the guess that a frame
alternates between depth-using and depth-less draws often enough to end a batch
constantly. It does not: surface re-uploads run at about 1.7 per frame. With
batching on, the flushes per frame should therefore be a handful, not
thousands, and a race between a handful of command buffers is a much poorer
explanation for specks scattered across a flat wall.

WHAT TO MEASURE INSTEAD, and it is one number: command buffers per frame on the
BATCHED path, from the same RECOMP_METAL_CB_STATS line. If it is a handful,
the residual is not the same race and needs its own explanation. If it is still
dozens, something is ending batches far more often than the surface churn
accounts for, and that something is the lead.


20. THE PIPELINE COMPARED STAGE BY STAGE, WHICH RULES OUT A WHOLE CLASS
========================================================================
Done because hypothesis-and-test had knocked down four mechanisms in a row and
a structural comparison finds OMISSIONS rather than bugs. Write out what an
NV2A-to-Metal translation must do, stage by stage, and ask of each stage
whether this implementation does it, refuses it, or silently ignores it. The
third category is the dangerous one.

    vertex fetch, T&L, viewport   implemented, shared vs between both paths
    clip and cull                 CPU side, shared
    texture sample, mips, DXT     implemented AND byte-exact in metal_copy_test
    register combiners            implemented, byte-exact
    alpha test                    implemented
    depth and stencil             implemented
    blend                         implemented
    dither                        implemented (stage order fixed today)
    fog                           refused
    logic op                      refused
    colour write mask             refused
    texture address modes         refused
    texture filter, format, LOD   refused
    polygon offset, window clip   refused
    multisample, shade mode       refused

THERE IS NO THIRD CATEGORY. nv2a_texture_copy_prepare refuses about thirty
distinct states by name rather than approximating any of them, which is the
right design and is why looking for a missing stage found nothing.

AND THE REFUSAL PATH NEVER FIRES HERE. Over four runs:

    [TEXTURE] prepared=750558 rejected=0
    [TEXTURE] prepared=792428 rejected=0
    [TEXTURE] prepared=440094 rejected=0
    [RASTER]  0 batches + 0 triangles on the CPU

Every draw this title issues is expressible, accepted and rendered by the sink.
Nothing is dropped, nothing falls back, nothing is approximated.

ONE REAL GAP FOUND, WHICH IS NOT THIS BUG. A draw the decoder rejects is
DROPPED, not rasterised on the CPU: nv2a_pb_exec.c:2944 logs the first eight
and returns. It is counted in neither gpu_fallbacks nor cpu_batches, which is
why both read zero and why nobody would notice. For a title that used fog or a
colour mask, geometry would simply be absent with every counter reading clean.
JSRF never triggers it, so it is a latent hazard rather than the cause.

WHAT THIS LEAVES, and it is the useful half of a negative result. The residual
cannot be a PER-DRAW problem: every stage is implemented or refused, nothing is
ignored, no draw is dropped, and the per-draw translation is verified
byte-exact against the CPU oracle across combiners, alpha test, stencil,
multi-texture, DXT and mips. So it has to be about how draws COMBINE or
PERSIST -- the retained surface across frames, or ordering between passes.

That is the same place the tile mosaic lived, which is consistent with a person
watching it saying the residual looks like the same issue. It differs in one
measured respect: the mosaic sat on a clean 64 grid and this does not. Seam
spacings in the corrupted region are 12.1, 4.3, 9.8, 12.1, 2.5, 5.6, 2.0, 1.7,
32.0 -- irregular. I had called it "the same class at finer granularity" from a
magnified image before measuring, and the measurement does not support it.

```

`docs/jsrf/oracle-evidence/2026-09-12_clock2000_zero_divergence/README.md`:

```md
# Zero-divergence dump pair — Windows vs macOS at guest clock ~2000

Preserved as evidence. Do not regenerate these files; take new anchors as new
directories beside this one.

## What was compared

| file | host | build | guest clock at dump |
|---|---|---|---|
| `windows_clang_clock2006.json` | Windows (CrossOver, bottle `recomp-gate`) | clang/mingw, native TLS (`tools/windows/clang-mingw.cmake`) | **2006** |
| `macos_metal_clock2008.json` | macOS arm64 | clang, `RECOMP_METAL=1` | **2008** |
| `macos_metal_clock2132_runB.json` | macOS arm64 | same as above, second run | **2132** |

Guest clock = entries to `sub_000123E0`, the manager's per-frame tick, counted
by `jsrf_func_hit` and read with `jsrf_func_hit_count()`. Both hosts ran the
**same gen tree** and the same recompiled guest code.

## Method

    RECOMP_OBJECT_DUMP=<dir> RECOMP_OBJECT_DUMP_AT=2000

`jsrf_object_dump()` writes the inventory once, when the clock first reaches
the requested value. Comparison is
`diagnostics/jsrf_first_fault/compare_objects.py A.json B.json`, which resolves
pointer-valued fields **symbolically** (to the id of the object pointed at) so
that two different heap layouts do not read as divergence. Vtables are compared
raw, because the XBE is mapped at the same VA on both hosts.

## Result

    root address     0x040d3a70 on BOTH hosts (delta +0x0)
    manager          all 12 compared fields identical
    id set           identical, 9 ids
    per-object       every common object matches on every compared field
    -> 0 divergent field group(s)

Compared ranges: manager fields `live, skip_draw, draw_mode, state_7930,
state_7934, state_7EC4, exec_root, draw_root, draw_root_tail, draw_sort_root,
draw_sort_tail, draw_sort_bins`; per object `vtable, flags, stored_id,
draw_child_mask, zsort_key, zsort, extra_44, extra_48, parent, child,
sibling_before, sibling_next, draw_next, draw_before_ptr, draw_last_ptr,
fz, tx, ty, tz`.

## Noise floor (same host, two runs)

macOS run A (clock 2008) against macOS run B (clock 2132): **3 divergent field
groups** — `zsort` and `extra_44`, which hold heap pointers but sit in the
comparator's RAW list so two heaps disagree by construction, and one `tx`
float differing by -0.0000.

So the same-host noise floor is *worse* than the cross-host result at this
anchor. Anything above 3 field groups at a later anchor is signal.

## What this does NOT establish

* Nothing about the **tutorial**. Clock 2000 is before the title teardown
  (~2400). The Corn sequence is much later and has not been compared.
* Nothing about Windows being a correct control. At the deepest point measured
  Windows reaches **12 of 17** CPlayer gameplay markers where macOS reaches
  17 of 17. That gap is unexplained and must be resolved before Windows is
  trusted as a known-good reference for anything in gameplay.

```

`docs/jsrf/plans/CODEX_PERFORMANCE_BUG_HUNT_2026-09-14.md`:

```md
# Performance bug hunt, 14 September 2026

Read-only runtime review; no new gameplay run or performance A/B was performed.
Runtime files were being updated during review. The deferred-vblank retry and
explicit ISR-entry result are now present; the older review findings should
not be carried forward as if those changes were absent.

## Evidence and limits

`render-investigation/irq-new-3/stderr.log` ends with windows around 42 ms/frame:
8.2 ms vertex preparation, 9.0 ms submission, 3.3 ms sync, 22 ms residual.
Residual is not guest CPU time: it includes waiting and untimed runtime work.

`render-investigation/bimodal-1/stderr.log`, around t=36 s, reports 572 batches
per frame, 119.14 ms vertex preparation, 80.07 ms submission, 5.17 ms sync,
53.41 ms residual. USB TD retirements and WDH clears are progressing at this
point. This is an attract-screen observation, not a gameplay benchmark.
The log starts with translator=deadbeefdeadbeef and a STALE warning. This
appears to be the manifest negative control; establish provenance before
using this run as a clean baseline. It does not prove the translated code is
actually stale, but the current stamp cannot establish that it is current.

Stage timers surround entire calls and measure elapsed time, including host
descheduling. Their window totals reset at report time while frame intervals
are recorded at flips, so a short window can straddle partial frames. Prefer
several stable windows and a profile of the rendering thread.

## Main performance targets

1. **CPU vertex interpretation, repeated per index occurrence.**
   `src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c:prepare_vertices` traverses `idx_count`, fetches
   attributes and calls `nv2a_vsh_execute` each time. There is no within-batch
   transformed-vertex cache. Measure indices versus unique indices first;
   cache complete transformed outputs for repeated indices in eligible
   indexed draws, with batch-local lifetime. Validate identical outputs,
   including colours and texture coordinates, and preserve inline-vertex
   semantics. Larger follow-up: specialise decoded programs or translate them
   to Metal; do not start with that larger correctness surface.

2. **A Metal command buffer and encoder per draw.**
   `src/nv2a/nv2a_metal.m:nv2a_metal_draw` creates a command buffer, creates an
   encoder, binds state, ends encoding and commits for each batch. Hundreds
   of draws imply hundreds of submissions per frame. Measure command creation,
   encoding, commit and ring wait separately. Experiment with multiple ordered
   draws per command buffer, flushing at sync/readback and required resource
   transitions. Preserve attachment visibility, guest surface coherence and
   staging-buffer lifetime. Existing slab staging does not remove this cost.

3. **Texture cache hits still read all texture bytes.**
   `texture_buffer` validates hits with full `memcmp`. High hit rate means
   few uploads, not cheap validation. Count bytes compared and elapsed time.
   Avoid caching by pointer alone: guest writes must invalidate cached data.
   A trustworthy dirty-generation scheme is a later optimisation if bandwidth
   measurement warrants it.

## Correctness bugs that can damage pacing

4. **Interrupt scheduling state is shared but no longer protected by default.**
   `bridge_vblank_poll` has shared non-atomic `next_vblank`; the step helper
   has shared `carry_us`. `bridge_device_irq_poll` has shared `next_irq`.
   The global lock only runs in legacy mode; per-vector claims happen later.
   Concurrent waiters can race the deadline check/update even when ISR entry
   itself is exclusive. Protect deadline ownership independently of ISR/DPC
   execution. Test two callers at the same deadline and during a slow ISR.

5. **Deadline drift and coarse retry.**
   Both pumps schedule their next deadline from `now`, incorporating every
   late poll into future timing. Vblank retries also sit behind the next-frame
   deadline. Use a monotonic high-resolution phase and explicitly account for
   missed periods without blindly issuing catch-up interrupts. Test repeated
   late polls and measure wake latency, rather than only average ISR rate.

6. **Auto-reset event consumption is non-atomic and waits poll.**
   `bridge_KeWaitForSingleObject` reads SignalState and then separately writes
   zero. Two waiters can consume one signal; a concurrent set between the read
   and reset can be overwritten. `bridge_KeSetEvent` also uses plain accesses.
   Serialize event state with a host wait mechanism or consistent atomics and
   a wake protocol. Test two waiters/one signal and set-versus-consume races.
   Preserve notification-event semantics and interrupt pumping while blocked.
   Reducing the sleep interval further does not fix these races.

## Suggested order

First establish a valid, scene-confirmed baseline and profile the active render
thread; do not infer CPU idleness from a whole-process tally of blocked workers.
Fix deadline/event races with focused concurrent tests. Then A/B vertex reuse
and command-buffer batching separately. Keep USB/WDH investigation separate
unless time-aligned evidence links it to the frame slowdown. Record frame
latency distributions, sound-server rate, TD retirements and image correctness.

The code and existing logs support substantial CPU-side rendering costs and
fragile scheduling. They do not yet establish the cause of the bimodal split
or quantify the speedup any proposed change will deliver.

```

`docs/jsrf/plans/GPU_VERTEX_SHADING.md`:

```md
# Moving the NV2A vertex program off the CPU

16 Sep 2026. How `nv2a_vsh_msl.c` gets wired into `nv2a_metal.m`, written after
establishing that the emitter computes the right thing. **This document does not
implement anything.** It exists so that the implementation in `nv2a_metal.m` can
be written once.

The measurement that motivates it, gameplay, per frame:

    vsh 7.00 + submit 5.69 + sync 5.08 + clear 0.25 + rest 3.35 = 21.37 ms

Against a 16.67 ms budget. `vsh` is `prepare_vertices()` in
`src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c`, which runs the guest's vertex program on the CPU
once per index per draw, about 700,000 draws in a 280 s run.

---

## 1. What is now known about the emitter, and what is not

`src/nv2a/nv2a_vsh_msl.c` had never been executed. Its own header said so.
`diagnostics/jsrf_first_fault/vsh_msl_diff_test.m` now dispatches the emitted
code on a real device and diffs all sixteen output registers against
`nv2a_vsh_execute`, over **the 126 distinct vertex programs read out of the
title's own `default.xbe`** plus one synthetic program per opcode.

    title corpus   126 programs   8064 vectors   0 residual disagreements
    synthetic      21 programs    1303 vectors   0 residual disagreements

Three real defects came out of it and are fixed in `nv2a_vsh_msl.c`:

| defect | how it showed | fix |
|---|---|---|
| Metal fuses `a*b+c` into an fma even under `MTLMathModeSafe`; the interpreter does not, because `multiply()`'s zero test is a select | 51 of 8064 vectors, up to 1.78 absolute in clip space, concentrated in seven skinning programs | `#pragma clang fp contract(off)` in the preamble |
| NV2A's rule that `a*0` and `0*b` are `+0` even against infinity was not reproduced | a zero normal takes `rsqrt(0) = +inf` into the normalise multiply: NaN on the GPU, `0` on the CPU, and the NaN reaches `oPos` | `vsh_mul()` helper on MUL and MAD |
| `LIT` used `exp2(w * log2(max(y,0) + 1e-30))` with a bound of 128 | 59 of 64 fixture vectors; any `y <= 0` with a negative exponent | `pow()` and the interpreter's `127.99609375` bound |

**The limits of that evidence, which the implementation has to respect:**

- **`DPH`, `DST`, `EXP`, `LOG`, `LIT` appear in no program this title ships.**
  Their only evidence is a synthetic fixture built with `vsh_encode.h`. If a
  program containing one ever reaches the GPU path, it is untested against the
  title.
- **The emitted screen-space epilogue is checked against a *reading* of
  `prepare_vertices()` and of the fixed `vs` in `nv2a_metal.m`, not against the
  renderer.** FULL mode in the diff test agrees to 1.65e-06, which says the
  transcription is faithful to that reading. It does not say the reading is
  right. Nothing has been rendered.
- **Nothing has been drawn.** `nv2a_metal.m` does not call the emitter, and the
  emitter's header still says so.
- 13 of 8064 title vectors disagree by up to 4.3e-04 relative on `oPos`. The
  test's conditioning probe shows the interpreter's own answer moves that far
  under a one-ulp change to its operands, so these are the programs' own
  conditioning, not the emitter's. **They are still real divergences in the
  rendered image** — see §7 on what that means for an A/B.

---

## 2. The shape of the change

Today:

    pushbuffer -> prepare_vertices()  fetch attrs, run program per index,
                                      snap to 1/16, write s_outputs[i][16][4]
               -> nv2a_metal_draw(state, ..., s_outputs, count, primitive)
               -> vs()  screen -> clip, pass through d0/d1/t0..t3
               -> fs()/fs_hw()/fs_hw_blend()

After:

    pushbuffer -> nv2a_metal_set_vsh(words, length, constants)   [new]
               -> nv2a_metal_draw_indexed(state, attrs, indices, count, ...)
               -> vsh_main()  the guest's own program, then the same
                              screen -> clip the emitter already emits
               -> fs()/fs_hw()/fs_hw_blend()  unchanged

`prepare_vertices()` keeps existing and keeps running whenever the GPU path
refuses (§6). It is not deleted, and it is the thing the new path is scored
against.

The vertex stage the emitter produces already absorbs both pieces of fixed work
that sit on either side of the interpreter today — the 1/16 subpixel snap from
`prepare_vertices()` and the screen-to-clip divide from `vs()`. That is
deliberate and is why the generated function can replace `vs` outright rather
than feeding it.

---

## 3. A program becomes an MTLFunction

### 3.1 Two caches, not one

`hw_pipeline_for()` keys pipelines on `(blend, blend_src, blend_dst, sblend)`.
That key now gains two more dimensions — which vertex program, and which vertex
layout — and the product of three independent sets does not belong in one flat
table. So:

**Cache A: microcode -> MTLFunction.** Compiling MSL is the expensive half
(`newLibraryWithSource:` is a full front end) and it depends on nothing but the
program. Keyed on the microcode words.

**Cache B: (function, layout, blend key) -> MTLRenderPipelineState.** Keyed on
Cache A's slot index, a layout id (§5.3) and the existing four blend fields.
This is `hw_pipeline_for` with a wider key, and it should stay that function's
shape: a fixed-size linear array, a miss counter, and a refusal when full.

### 3.2 Cache A, concretely

```c
#define VSH_CACHE 192          /* see the sizing note below */
static struct {
    uint32_t words[NV2A_VS_MAX_INSTRUCTIONS][4];
    int      length;
    uint32_t hash;             /* FNV-1a, for the fast reject only */
    id<MTLFunction> fn;
    int      refused;          /* the emitter said no; do not retry */
    unsigned long long uses;
} vsh_fn[VSH_CACHE];
static unsigned vsh_fn_n;
```

A lookup hashes the words, scans for a matching hash, and then **compares the
words in full**. `trace_selected_program()` in `nv2a_pb_exec.c` already
identifies programs by a 32-bit FNV hash and nothing has ever collided, which is
not the same as nothing ever colliding; a cache that hands a draw the wrong
vertex program produces wrong geometry with no error anywhere. The full compare
costs at most 136 * 16 bytes on a hit and is off the per-vertex path entirely.

**Sizing, from a measurement rather than a guess.** The image contains 126
distinct programs (`vsh_xbe_corpus.h`, cross-checked against the title's own
length table: 123 of the 126 carry a matching `(slots<<16)|0x2078` header).
`RECOMP_VSH_TRACE` reports distinct selected programs at runtime but caps its
own table at 32, so it has never been able to say whether a session uses all
126. 192 holds every program in the image with room; it is 192 * (2176 + a
pointer), about 420 KB, once, for a path that would otherwise recompile.

**A full cache must not evict.** Evicting an `MTLFunction` throws away a
compile that will be wanted again next frame, and `newLibraryWithSource:` on
the draw thread is exactly the stall this change exists to remove. If the cache
fills, count it and send the draw to the CPU. The report says so (§8) and the
number to watch is that it stays zero.

**A refusal is cached too.** `nv2a_vsh_generate_msl()` returning 0 is a property
of the program, not of the draw. Re-emitting and re-failing 700,000 times would
cost more than the interpreter. The `refused` flag makes it once per program.

### 3.3 When Cache A is filled

On the draw thread, at the point `prepare_vertices()` would decode: if
`s_vsh.dirty` cleared and the decode succeeded, hash the selected words and look
them up. A miss runs `nv2a_vsh_generate_msl()`, then `newLibraryWithSource:`
with **`MTLCompileOptions.mathMode = MTLMathModeSafe`** — not the default.

That is not a style preference. `initialize()` already sets it for the fixed
shader, and the differential test measured the emitted code against the
interpreter under safe math only. Under fast math `rsqrt`, `pow` and the
reciprocals are different functions and the result in §1 does not transfer.

Compilation is synchronous and will stall the first draw that uses a program.
126 programs at a few milliseconds each is a fraction of a second spread over a
session's first appearance of each shader, but it is a visible hitch at the
moment a new one appears. If that shows up in a frame trace, the fix is to
compile on a worker and use the interpreter until the function is ready — which
the fallback in §6 already provides for free. Do not build that first; measure
whether it is needed.

---

## 4. The constant file

The guest writes `c0..c191` through `NV097_SET_TRANSFORM_CONSTANT` and
`nv2a_pb_exec.c` keeps them in `s_vsh.constants[192][4]`. For skinned geometry
they change **between draws**, so they are per-draw state, not per-program
state.

The emitter declares them as `constant float4 *c [[buffer(1)]]`, 192 entries,
**3072 bytes**. That is inside Metal's 4 KB `setVertexBytes` limit, and the file
comment in `nv2a_vsh_msl.c` records that this is why the constant file is 192
and not the hardware's 256: 256 float4 is 4096 bytes, over the limit, and would
need a real `MTLBuffer` and a staging allocation per draw.

So: **`[encoder setVertexBytes:constants length:3072 atIndex:1]`, once per
draw.** No allocation, no ring reservation, no lifetime question.

**Buffer index 1 currently holds `Params` on the vertex stage.** The existing
encoder line binds vertex buffer 0 = vertices, 1 = `Params`, 2 = indices. The
generated function does not use `Params` at all — everything it needs is in the
constant file and the viewport block — so on a generated-program pipeline,
vertex buffer 1 is the constant file and vertex buffer 2 is `VSH_Viewport`.
`Params` stays at *fragment* buffer 1, which is a separate namespace and is
untouched. **The two pipelines have incompatible vertex bindings and the encoder
must not set both.** Getting this wrong is silent: the shader reads whatever is
bound and produces geometry.

`VSH_Viewport` is `{ width, height, depth }` — `NV097_SET_SURFACE_CLIP`'s width
and height and the 16777215 z divisor — the same three values `vs()` reads out
of `Params` today. 12 bytes, `setVertexBytes` at index 2.

The a0-relative read is emitted as `c[min((a0 + N) & 255, 191)]`. The 8-bit wrap
is hardware behaviour and matches `read_source()`. **The clamp is not**: the
interpreter refuses the whole draw when the wrapped index lands in 192..255, and
a vertex function cannot refuse. Across 8064 vectors of the title's own programs
the interpreter never refused for this reason, so it is not known to happen —
but "not observed in a synthetic sweep" is not "cannot happen", and §6's
counters are where it would show up if the clamp ever starts mattering.

---

## 5. Vertex attributes

This is the part with the least evidence behind it and the most room to be
wrong.

### 5.1 What the guest declares

`VertexAttr` in `nv2a_pb_exec.c` is `{ offset, type, size, stride }` per
attribute, sixteen of them, where `offset` is a **guest address** and `type` is
the NV097 format nibble. `fetch_attr()` decodes exactly three:

    TYPE_F       (2)  1..4 floats
    TYPE_UB_D3D  (0)  4 bytes B,G,R,A -> /255
    TYPE_UB_OGL  (4)  1..4 bytes      -> /255

and returns 0 for `S1`, `S32K` and `CMP`, which rejects the draw. Anything the
CPU path cannot fetch, the GPU path must also refuse — **not** silently produce
something else.

### 5.2 The mapping to Metal

`[[stage_in]]` with an `MTLVertexDescriptor`, which is what
`vsh_msl_compile_test.m` already builds and links against. The formats line up:

    TYPE_F size 1..4    -> MTLVertexFormatFloat, Float2, Float3, Float4
    TYPE_UB_OGL size 4  -> MTLVertexFormatUChar4Normalized
    TYPE_UB_D3D size 4  -> MTLVertexFormatUChar4Normalized_BGRA
    everything else     -> refuse the draw, count it by type

`UChar4Normalized_BGRA` reproduces `fetch_attr`'s channel order exactly. Confirm
that against a rendered frame before believing it: a swapped colour channel is
the kind of thing this project has got wrong from reading before
(`nv2a_metal.m`'s B5G6R5 note is the same mistake in the other direction, and it
cost a measurement to find).

A component count below 4 needs care. `fetch_attr` zeroes the components it does
not read and sets `w = 1`; Metal's `Float2` fills `z = 0, w = 1` for a `float4`
stage_in member, which is the same. `UChar4Normalized` has no 1/2/3-component
normalized-byte equivalent that matches, so **refuse `UB_OGL` with `size != 4`**
rather than approximate it.

### 5.3 Where the bytes come from

The guest's arrays live in the mapped guest RAM region. Two options:

**(a) Wrap guest RAM once.** `newBufferWithBytesNoCopy:` over the guest memory
region gives one `MTLBuffer` in which every attribute is an `offset` and a
`stride`, bound with `setVertexBuffer:offset:atIndex:`. No copy, no gather, no
per-draw allocation — the whole 7 ms goes away rather than shrinking. The
requirements are that the region is page-aligned and that its length is a
multiple of the page size, and that nothing unmaps or re-protects it under the
GPU. **That last one is not a small caveat in this tree**: CLAUDE.md's
guarded-MMIO rule exists because a thread unprotecting a page cost 13.5M lost
writes. Whether the guest RAM region is stable enough to hand to the GPU for the
lifetime of a command buffer is an open question and must be answered by
measurement, not by reading the allocator.

**(b) Gather into the existing staging ring.** Walk the batch's indices and copy
each used attribute's bytes into a packed interleaved buffer, then bind that.
This is a memcpy per attribute per index and it keeps a real share of the
current cost — it removes the *program execution* but not the *fetch*. It has no
lifetime question at all: the ring already solves that, with a self-test
(`metal_ring_test`).

**Do (b) first.** It is strictly less risky, it is bounded by machinery that
already exists and is tested, and it answers the question that actually matters
— how much of the 7 ms is the program and how much is the fetch — which nothing
currently knows. Then decide whether (a) is worth its risk.

Attribute buffer indices must avoid 1 and 2. Use 3 upward, one per used
attribute (`program->inputs_read` says which), or a single interleaved buffer at
index 3 under (b).

### 5.4 Indices

Today `vs()` does its own index lookup: `Vertex x = v[indices[id]]` with a
`device uint*` at buffer 2 and `drawPrimitives`. A `[[stage_in]]` function
cannot do that — the vertex fetch happens before the shader runs — so the
generated path must use `drawIndexedPrimitives:indexCount:indexType:
indexBuffer:indexBufferOffset:`. The index array is already staged in the ring.
`MTLIndexTypeUInt16` matches `s_gpu.idx`'s `uint16_t`; the assembly array is
12288 entries, well inside it.

This is a second behavioural difference between the two pipelines and a second
thing that has to be got right per pipeline rather than per encoder.

---

## 6. What happens when the emitter refuses

**This is the part that must be designed rather than discovered.** Today
`prepare_vertices()` has five named ways to fail and `note_vsh_reject()` counts
each one separately with the first offending detail. All five still exist. A
vertex function has none of them: it cannot return "no", and a program it cannot
express is a program that must not reach it.

`nv2a_vsh_generate_msl()` returns 0 for: a null or invalid program, no `FINAL`,
a write to the constant file, or a buffer too small. `nv2a_vsh_parse()` sets
`valid = 0` for an out-of-range opcode, temp or output register. Compilation and
pipeline creation can fail for anything. Attribute formats can be undecodable.
The caches can be full.

**Every one of those sends the draw to `prepare_vertices()` and the existing
`vs`/`fs` pipeline, and every one is counted under its own name.** The decision
is per draw and it is made before any GPU work is encoded, so there is never a
half-transformed batch.

    gpu_vsh_eligible(draw):
        if (!vsh_on())                     -> cpu, reason "switch off"
        if (s_vsh.mode != 2)               -> cpu, reason "fixed function"
        if (!decoded.valid || !has_final)  -> cpu, reason "undecodable program"
        if (cacheA[slot].refused)          -> cpu, reason "emitter refused"
        if (cacheA full)                   -> cpu, reason "program cache full"
        if (library/function failed)       -> cpu, reason "compile failed"
        for each attribute in inputs_read:
            if (!format_supported(type,size)) -> cpu, reason "attribute format"
        if (cacheB full || pipeline failed)-> cpu, reason "pipeline"
        -> gpu

The reason table should be the same shape as `s_vsh_reject[]`: reason strings as
literals compared by pointer, a fixed-size table, and the first offending detail
kept. "38,472 rejected" named no cause and could not be acted on; that lesson is
already written into `nv2a_pb_exec.c` and this arm should not have to learn it
again.

**The fallback must be a fallback, not a silent second renderer.** A frame that
takes the CPU path for some draws and the GPU path for others is running two
different vertex stages with two different rounding behaviours (§1), into one
depth buffer. `nv2a_metal.m` already has exactly this hazard named for the
fragment stage — `g_hw_mixed`, "MIXED draws (software tail while hw on)" — and
the vertex stage needs the same counter for the same reason.

---

## 7. `RECOMP_METAL_VSH`

Opt-in, off by default, read through **`recomp_switch_on()` from
`src/recomp_switch.h`**:

```c
#include "recomp_switch.h"
static int vsh_on(void)
{
    static int on = -1;
    if (on < 0) on = recomp_switch_on("RECOMP_METAL_VSH");
    return on;
}
```

Not `getenv(...) != NULL`. That header exists because three switches here were
presence-tested and their control arms ran with the guard on —
`RECOMP_APU_SELFLINK_END`, `RECOMP_VSH_REUSE` and `RECOMP_PB_EXEC` — and the
obvious way to take the control arm of this A/B is `RECOMP_METAL_VSH=0`, which a
presence test reads as ON. Read once and cache: the switch cannot change during
a run and `getenv` on the draw path is a cost for nothing.

**A second switch, `RECOMP_METAL_VSH_VERIFY`, also boolean, also through
`recomp_switch_on()`.** With it set, the GPU path runs *and* `prepare_vertices()`
runs, and the two transformed vertex sets are compared on the CPU, component by
component, with the first few disagreements printed by draw, index, register and
component. It is far slower than either arm and is not a mode anyone plays in.

It is the whole reason to believe this change. `vsh_msl_diff_test.m` compares the
two implementations on synthetic operand data; VERIFY compares them on the
title's actual vertices, its actual constants and its actual a0 values — which is
the only place the 4.3e-04 conditioning divergences and the constant-index clamp
can be shown to matter or not to. Build it at the same time as the fast path,
not after.

---

## 8. What the `[METAL]` report must print

`ab_score.py` refuses to compare two arms that report the same switch state, and
it can only check a switch that names itself. Every line below prints
unconditionally, in both arms, in `nv2a_metal_report()`:

```
[METAL] vsh: %s (metal_vsh %s, verify %s)
        -> "GPU vertex programs" / "CPU interpreter", then the two switch
           states as read, not as intended. This line is what names the arm.

[METAL] vsh draws: %llu GPU, %llu CPU, %llu MIXED frames
        -> the split. MIXED counts frames in which both paths ran, which is
           the hazard in section 6, not a statistic.

[METAL] vsh vertices: %llu transformed on GPU, %llu on CPU
        -> the number the 7.00 ms is proportional to. A GPU draw count that
           moves while this stays at zero means the counter is on the wrong
           side of the branch.

[METAL] vsh programs: %llu distinct, %llu cache hits, %llu compiles,
        %llu compile failures, %llu emitter refusals, %llu cache-full
        -> "distinct" is the population of cache A and should settle well
           under 126. "compiles" should stop growing after the first minute
           of a session; if it does not, the key is wrong and the cache is
           thrashing. "cache-full" must stay 0 or VSH_CACHE is too small.

[METAL] vsh pipelines: %llu built, %llu cache hits, %llu refusals
        -> the same three hw_pipeline_for already reports, for the wider key.
           Refusals must stay 0; each one is a draw on the CPU.

[METAL] vsh CPU fallback by reason: <literal>=%llu (detail %u) ...
        -> the s_vsh_reject[] shape. Eight slots, reason strings compared by
           pointer, first detail retained. Without this, a fallback count is
           a number with no action attached to it.

[METAL] vsh attribute formats refused: type%u size%u = %llu ...
        -> S1, S32K and CMP are undecoded on BOTH paths today. If one of them
           ever appears this says which, which is what decides whether it is
           worth implementing.

[METAL] vsh verify: %llu vertices compared, %llu components differed,
        worst %.3g relative, first at draw %u index %u o%d.%c
        -> only under RECOMP_METAL_VSH_VERIFY. THE POSITIVE CONTROL FOR THE
           WHOLE ARM: "0 differed" means the two vertex stages agree only if
           "compared" is large. Print both or the zero proves nothing.
```

**Every absence-measurement here needs its positive control.** `GPU draws` being
large is the control for `CPU draws` being small; `vertices compared` being large
is the control for `components differed` being zero; the reason table being
populated is the control for a fallback count that is not zero. A report that
prints only the zeros is the failure mode this project keeps paying for.

---

## 9. How to know it worked

The frame decomposition already exists and already separates `vsh`. The A/B is:

    RECOMP_METAL_VSH=0 ... jsrf_first_fault    control
    RECOMP_METAL_VSH=1 ... jsrf_first_fault    arm

One pinned binary, one pad script, run serially, and check the binary hash
changed between builds before believing any difference — same-second mtimes have
silently produced four identical "different" arms in this tree before.

Expected: `vsh` falls towards zero and `submit` rises, because the work moved
rather than vanished, and the net is whatever the GPU does with it. **A drop in
`vsh` with no change in total frame time is a real possible outcome** and would
mean the draw thread was never the bottleneck — which is worth knowing and is
not a failure of this document.

Before that A/B is meaningful, three things must be true and each is a separate
check:

1. `RECOMP_METAL_VSH_VERIFY=1` over a real mission reports `components
   differed = 0` with `vertices compared` in the millions. This is the claim
   `vsh_msl_diff_test.m` cannot make, because it uses synthetic operands.
2. The `[METAL]` report shows `CPU draws = 0` — or names every reason it is not.
3. A frame captured with the arm on is compared against the control by the
   `x0 mod 4` structural score already used for the fragment-path work, not by
   eye. Six image metrics failed on the last artefact here before one worked.

---

## 10. Files

| file | role |
|---|---|
| `src/nv2a/nv2a_vsh_msl.c` | the emitter. Checked against the interpreter; still never drawn with. |
| `src/nv2a/nv2a_vsh.c` | the interpreter. The reference, and the fallback. Unchanged. |
| `src/nv2a/nv2a_metal.m` | where all of section 3 to 8 goes. Not touched by this document. |
| `src/kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c` | `prepare_vertices()`, `s_vsh`, the reject table. The branch in section 6 starts here. |
| `diagnostics/jsrf_first_fault/vsh_msl_diff_test.m` | the differential test. Run it after any emitter change. |
| `diagnostics/jsrf_first_fault/vsh_xbe_corpus.h` | reads the title's 126 programs out of `default.xbe` at run time. Needs `JSRF_GAME_DIR`. |
| `diagnostics/jsrf_first_fault/vsh_msl_compile_test.m` | does the emitted text compile and link against a vertex layout. |

```
